main.summary: Animal Farm (originally Animal Farm: A Fairy Story) is a satirical, allegorical, dystopian novella and beast fable by George Orwell, first published in England on 17 August 1945.

cards.heading: Animal Farm
cards.text:
Animal Farm (originally Animal Farm: A Fairy Story) is a satirical, allegorical, dystopian novella and beast fable by George Orwell, first published in England on 17 August 1945. It follows the mistreated, anthropomorphized farm animals of Manor Farm as they rebel against their human master and endeavor to create a utopian society. However, the rebellion is hijacked and betrayed, and under the dictatorship of the pigs, the farm ends up in a dystopian state nearly identical to what it had been before.

According to Orwell, Animal Farm was inspired by events leading up to the Russian Revolution of 1917 and then the Stalinist era of the Soviet Union, a period when Russia lived under the Marxist–Leninist ideology of Joseph Stalin. Orwell, a democratic socialist, was a critic of Stalin and hostile to Moscow-directed Stalinism, an attitude that was critically shaped by his experiences during the Barcelona May Day conflicts between the POUM and Stalinist forces during the Spanish Civil War.

main.title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
main.summary: The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and Nagasaki on 9 August, during the final days of World War II.

cards.heading: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
cards.text: The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and Nagasaki on 9 August, during the final days of World War II. The attacks killed an estimated 150,000 to 246,000 people, most of them civilians. The Manhattan Project had produced two different weapons: Little Boy used enriched uranium, while Fat Man used plutonium in an implosion design. Specially equipped B-29 aircraft carried them from Tinian in the Mariana Islands. The bombings remain the only use of nuclear weapons in armed conflict.

main.title: United Nations
main.summary: The UN Charter was signed on 26 June 1945, establishing a framework for international peace, security and cooperation.

cards.heading: United Nations
cards.text:
The United Nations (UN) is an international intergovernmental organization established by the signing of the Charter of the United Nations on 26 June 1945 with the articulated mission of maintaining international peace and security, to develop friendly relations among states, to promote international cooperation, and to serve as a centre for harmonizing the actions of states in achieving those goals.

The United Nations headquarters is located in New York City, with several other offices located in Geneva, Nairobi, Vienna and The Hague. The UN comprises six principal organizations: General Assembly, Security Council, Economic and Social Council, International Court of Justice, Secretariat and Trusteeship Council which, together with several specialized agencies and related agencies, make up the UN System. There is a total of 193 member states, representing nearly all of the world's sovereign states, as well as two observer states, the Holy See and the State of Palestine.

cards.heading: ENIAC is publicly dedicated
cards.text:
ENIAC was publicly dedicated in 1946, following its completion in 1945. Designed by John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert, it combined electronic operation with programmability to tackle a wide range of numerical problems.

ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer) was the first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer, completed in 1945. Other computers had some of these features, but ENIAC was the first to have them all. ENIAC was Turing-complete and able to solve "a large class of numerical problems" through reprogramming.

ENIAC was designed by Ursinus College physics professor John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert of the University of Pennsylvania to calculate artillery firing tables for the United States Army's Ballistic Research Laboratory (which later became a part of the Army Research Laboratory). However, its first program was a study of the feasibility of the thermonuclear weapon.

ENIAC was completed in 1945 and first put to work for practical purposes on December 10, 1945.

main.title: Roswell incident
main.summary: Debris found by a rancher in 1947 near Roswell, New Mexico, has become the basis for UFO conspiracy theories alleging that the United States military recovered a crashed extraterrestrial spacecraft.

cards.heading: Roswell incident
cards.text:
Debris found by a rancher in 1947 near Roswell, New Mexico, has become the basis for UFO conspiracy theories alleging that the United States military recovered a crashed extraterrestrial spacecraft. After metallic and rubber debris was recovered by Roswell Army Air Field personnel, the United States Army Air Forces announced possession of a "flying disc". This announcement made international headlines, but was retracted within a day. In reality, the debris was from a complex uncrewed military balloon train, consisting of linked balloons and assorted equipment, operated from the nearby Alamogordo Army Air Field as part of the top-secret Project Mogul, a program intended to detect Soviet nuclear tests. To obscure the purpose and source of the debris, the army reported that it was merely a conventional weather balloon. 

In 1978, retired United States Air Force officer Jesse Marcel claimed that the Army's weather balloon claim had been a cover story, and speculated that the debris was of extraterrestrial origin.

main.title: Transistor
main.summary: Bell Labs produced the first working transistor in 1947 through the work of John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley.

cards.heading: Transistor
cards.text: Bell Labs produced the first working transistor in 1947 through the work of John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley. Their point-contact device used a small electrical input to control a larger current, allowing signals to be amplified or switched. Transistors became fundamental components of modern electronics, first as individual devices and later in great numbers inside integrated circuits. Earlier field-effect concepts had been proposed but could not yet be built. The three physicists shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for the achievement.

cards.heading: From Baltimore to the Atlantic
cards.text: Tom Clancy was born in Baltimore on 12 April 1947. He studied English at Loyola and worked in insurance before publishing The Hunt for Red October in 1984. Its central problem gives the military hardware a dramatic purpose: a Soviet submarine commander intends to defect, and the Americans must understand what he is doing before either navy destroys the opportunity. CIA analyst Jack Ryan became the recurring character through whom Clancy explored intelligence, political decisions and armed conflict.

cards.heading: Jack Ryan crosses into cinema
cards.text: The books brought readers into a world of submarines, surveillance and competing chains of command. Technical information matters because it changes what the characters can detect, infer and risk. The Hunt for Red October, Patriot Games, Clear and Present Danger and The Sum of All Fears later became films, taking Jack Ryan to a wider audience. Across those adaptations, the analyst moves between interpreting evidence and confronting the consequences of decisions made far above him.

cards.heading: Planning the next move
cards.text: Clancy also helped establish Red Storm Entertainment in 1996. The studio released Rainbow Six in 1998, bringing his name into a form of action built around preparation and coordinated teams. The novel and game shared a counterterrorist premise, while the game made planning and execution something the player had to manage. Ubisoft acquired Red Storm in 2000; Ghost Recon followed in 2001. These releases made the Clancy name a lasting presence in military games as well as fiction.

main.title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
main.summary: "A Mathematical Theory of Communication" is an article by mathematician Claude Shannon published in Bell System Technical Journal in 1948.

cards.heading: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
cards.text: "A Mathematical Theory of Communication" is an article by mathematician Claude Shannon published in Bell System Technical Journal in 1948. It was renamed The Mathematical Theory of Communication in the 1949 book of the same name, a small but significant title change after realizing the generality of this work. It has tens of thousands of citations, being one of the most influential and cited scientific papers of all time, as it gave rise to the field of information theory, with Scientific American referring to the paper as the "Magna Carta of the Information Age", while the electrical engineer Robert G. Gallager called the paper a "blueprint for the digital era". Historian James Gleick rated the paper as the most important development of 1948, placing the transistor second in the same time period, with Gleick emphasizing that the paper by Shannon was "even more profound and more fundamental" than the transistor.

main.title: Bicycle Thieves
main.subtitle: A father and son search Rome for the bicycle that supports their family
main.summary: Vittorio De Sica's Bicycle Thieves follows Antonio Ricci, a father who finds work putting up posters in post-war Rome. The job requires a bicycle, and its theft threatens the family's new income. Released in 1948, the film sends Antonio and his young son Bruno through the city in search of the missing machine.

cards.heading: A job depends on a bicycle
cards.text: Vittorio De Sica's Bicycle Thieves follows Antonio Ricci, a father who finds work putting up posters in post-war Rome. The job requires a bicycle, and its theft threatens the family's new income. Released in 1948, the film sends Antonio and his young son Bruno through the city in search of the missing machine.

cards.heading: The city in the search
cards.text: The search carries them through markets, streets and crowded public places. Each stop offers a possible lead and consumes time Antonio cannot easily spare. The bicycle joins a private worry to the city's larger shortage of secure work. Lamberto Maggiorani and Enzo Staiola play the father and son, and the use of non-professional performers and real locations gives their movements a close connection to everyday Rome. The narrative keeps returning to what the loss means for the household.

cards.heading: A father seen by his son
cards.text: Bruno changes how Antonio's struggle is seen. His presence makes the father's decisions part of a relationship, with trust and embarrassment alongside the immediate need for money. Small interruptions in the search allow their affection and unequal understanding of the danger to emerge. This concentration on ordinary lives helped make the film a central work of Italian neorealism. In 1952 it headed the first Sight and Sound critics' poll of the greatest films.

main.title: LP record
main.summary: Columbia Records introduced the long-playing vinyl record in 1948, establishing the 33⅓ rpm album format.

cards.heading: LP record
cards.text: The LP (from long playing or long play) is an analog sound storage medium, specifically a phonograph record format characterized by a speed of 33+1⁄3 rpm, a 12- or 10-inch (30- or 25-cm) diameter, use of the "microgroove" groove specification, and a black vinyl (a copolymer of vinyl chloride acetate) composition disk. Introduced by Columbia Records in 1948, it was soon adopted as a new standard by the entire US record industry and, apart from a few relatively minor refinements and the important later addition of stereophonic sound in 1957, it remained the standard format for record albums during a period in popular music known as the "album era". LP was originally a trademark of Columbia and competed against the smaller 7-inch sized "45" or "single" format by RCA Victor, eventually ending up on top. Today in the vinyl revival era, a large majority of records are based on the LP format, and hence the LP name continues to be in use today to refer to new records.
